content.title: About
content.content: Lamb or mutton is the meat of sheep, often served with a savory gravy made from broth, tomatoes and spices. Tender, juicy and slightly sweet, it is rich in protein and iron. Traditionally the dish is slow‑cooked so the meat becomes melt‑in‑your‑mouth and absorbs the sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb is one of the oldest meats consumed by humans.
Different cuisines have their own gravy styles: Indian curry, Mediterranean tomato‑olive sauce, or French red wine reduction.
Lamb is a staple of festive meals, such as Easter pilaf or Scottish haggis.
The meat is high in creatine, which supports muscle energy.
Traditionally lamb is cooked over open fire or in earthenware pots, giving it a distinctive flavor.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Lamb provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High in iron
items.content: Heme iron from lamb is easily absorbed, helping prevent anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12, niacin and riboflavin, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals boost immune health and protect against oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Lamb contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lamb proteins.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor bacteria such as Salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Lamb is rich in purines, which can be problematic for people with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve lamb with gravy over mashed potatoes, rice, couscous or fresh vegetables. Typically the meat is cut into chunks and simmered in the gravy for 2–3 hours until tender. It also works well baked in the oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh lamb in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen lamb can be stored at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or a gray color; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.
